A note from the detective's desk

Welcome to Quackford City.

In this world, a punctuation mark is a traffic signal, a new word is a clue, and every reading task brings us closer to solving a mystery. Detective Duck makes literacy practice feel like an adventure worth coming back to.

🔎

Look closer

Meet tricky words with a tap-to-learn picture dictionary and read them in the context of a mystery.

🚦

Find your rhythm

Watch commas and full stops become friendly pauses during oral reading.

🧩

Make sense of the story

Put clue cards in order, interview suspects and justify your answer.

🏆

Feel proud

Earn stars and badges, create an avatar and record a reflection after the case.

An invitation to investigate

The Golden Quill has disappeared.

Yesterday afternoon, the famous Golden Quill disappeared from the Quackford Museum. A black feather was found near its glass cabinet. Muddy footprints led into the garden. Who might know the truth?

Meet Professor Puddle, Lily Lark, Benny Beaver and Mr. Crow. Each has a story. Young detectives must read, ask, listen and think before pointing a finger.

Meet the suspects

The mystery of the missing Golden Quill

Read the opening case, meet six original hand-drawn characters and explore the clues before playing.

A rainy morning. A curious case.
Official case report

Read the evidence.

Yesterday afternoon, the famous Golden Quill disappeared from the Quackford Museum.

It was kept in a glass cabinet in the main room.

At four o'clock, the guard locked the door.

At half past four, a visitor named Crow ran out of the room.

A black feather lay by the cabinet.

Muddy footprints led to the garden.

Game text reproduced from the supplied HTML, with the apostrophe typeset for this page.

Detective's question

What makes a strong conclusion?

A careful detective does not guess. Pupils name a suspect, select relevant clues and explain their thinking using sentences such as:

“I think ____ because the evidence shows ____.”

Talk about the difference between a clue and proof.

Pupil pathway

🪪 My Detective Passport

Open the game and choose Pupil Sign In. Enter a teacher-assigned ID, nickname and class. Each pupil keeps a separate local game profile on a shared device.

Complete the case and Academy activities; open My Progress to see recorded attempts, successes and areas to practise. Use the Recording Studio to choose text, explicitly allow recording, listen back and export a portfolio.

Pupil: open the game
Teacher pathway

👩‍🏫 Class Progress Dashboard

Open the game and choose Teacher. Create a local teacher PIN. See each pupil's ID, class, practice attempts, incorrect answers, full question history, original writing and recordings saved or imported on that browser.

Open a pupil record to enter the CEFR level (Pre-A1 to A2), TP1–TP6 and observation notes. Download a CSV or class backup for school records.

Teacher: open the game
Making listening work

🔊 Listen, practise, record, reflect

🔊

1 · Hear the clue

Tap play; select a device voice, change the speaking speed, replay slowly or show the transcript for access needs.

🗣️

2 · Watch a witness speak

Character beaks and mouths animate while the selected character narrates. Animation follows speaking status, not phoneme-by-phoneme lip sync.

🎙️

3 · Record reading

Pupils deliberately start and stop short microphone recordings. Saved voice clips are optional and require browser and school permissions.

Sharing progress with your teacher

Shared classroom device: local pupil IDs and a teacher dashboard can collect and review practice history on the same browser.

Different pupil devices: pupils tap Export my portfolio and safely pass the resulting JSON file to the teacher, who chooses Import pupil files. Recordings are included when the device has saved them successfully.

Using more than one device: The game keeps progress on the current device. Pupils can export their work for the teacher to import; automatic class-wide synchronisation is not included.

Teacher assessment: Teachers review pupils’ answers and reading recordings before assigning proficiency and mastery levels.

Data transfer

Example teacher workflow

1
Teacher creates a class code convention, such as 3A-01. Pupils use that ID on their devices.
2
Pupils practise reading and writing, then select an audio text and record only with permission.
3
Each pupil exports a JSON learning portfolio. Teacher imports those files into their local teacher desk.
4
Teacher reviews incorrect answers, writings and recordings, assigns proficiency and notes next steps. Export CSV for school analysis.

Share pupil portfolios privately with the teacher.

CASE FILE 01 / 05

Identification of Learner Needs

Five interconnected learner needs, identified through observations of class 3 UMT in 2025.

Skill Challenges 5 observed reading needs
🔍Vocabulary

Unknown words make texts harder to understand.

🎤Fluency

Reading aloud can be slow or hesitant.

🚦Punctuation

Pupils may miss pauses at commas and full stops.

🧩Retelling

Pupils found it difficult to understand and retell what they read.

💛Confidence

Pupils were hesitant and lacked confidence when reading aloud.

Source of Information

Personal observation (2025): Pupils in class 3 UMT struggled with unfamiliar words, reading aloud and punctuation. This experience is supported by research on reading difficulties and the KSSR Year 3 English DSKP (Content Standards 3.2 and 3.3 as cited in the blueprint).

Identified Gap
NOW Limited word knowledge, hesitant reading, missed punctuation, difficulty retelling and low confidence.
↓
GOAL Recognise more words, read fluently with pauses, understand and retell a story with growing confidence.

Skill Challenges

What do our young readers find difficult?

In 2025, I observed pupils in class 3 UMT who had difficulty reading English. They knew relatively few words, read slowly or hesitantly, often overlooked commas and full stops, struggled to understand or retell a text, and lacked confidence when asked to read aloud. These five needs shaped the purpose of Detective Duck.

1 · Reading foundations

Building reading confidence, one clue at a time

Detective Duck responds to the five needs I observed in 3 UMT: vocabulary, fluency, punctuation, comprehension and retelling, and reading confidence. Pupils practise them through one connected detective mystery.

Reading challengeNeed or gapGame response
Vocabulary deficitPupils struggle with unfamiliar words and their meanings in context.Magnifying Glass Case Dictionary: simple explanations, visuals and listening support.
Slow oral readingHesitation and uncertain pronunciation may reduce fluency.Read-aloud model and optional browser speech recognition or manual practice.
Ignoring punctuationReading may continue without meaningful pauses.Visual red-stop and yellow-slow punctuation checkpoints.
Weak retellingPupils have difficulty organising events and explaining what happened.Case Timeline, witness questions and written detective reasoning.
Source of Information

Where the evidence comes from

Classroom observation

During my observations of class 3 UMT in 2025, pupils showed limited vocabulary, hesitant oral reading, missed commas and full stops, difficulties understanding or retelling texts, and low reading confidence.

Evidence type: informal qualitative classroom observation. No diagnostic scores or formal test results have been supplied. The blueprint also includes observation and reading-difficulty diagrams (Figures 1 and 2, page 3).

Research and curriculum

The learning problem is supported by the academic reading cited in the blueprint, together with the KSSR English Year 3 curriculum. The complete bibliography is available on the References page.

Explore the references
2 · Curriculum intent

Reading standards at the centre

KSSR English Year 3
3.2

Understand texts using reading strategies

Young readers can experience this Content Standard as a basis for contextual vocabulary, strategies and comprehension.

KSSR English Year 3
3.3

Read fiction and non-fiction with enjoyment

The game uses an immersive story and confidence-building practice as ways to encourage reading.

Identified Gap

From reading difficulties to reading confidence

Current challenges

In class 3 UMT (2025), I noticed difficulties with word meanings, reading pace, punctuation, understanding or retelling and confidence during oral reading.

Desired learning outcomes

Pupils recognise and understand key vocabulary, read with appropriate pacing and punctuation, comprehend and retell a short story, and feel more confident reading aloud.

The learning gap: the pupils observed in 3 UMT needed repeated, supportive opportunities to develop word knowledge, fluency, punctuation awareness, comprehension and reading confidence within one meaningful experience.

Respondents and Testing Location

Who tried the prototype — and where?

Three TESL trainee teachers tested the prototype: two completed the trial online, while one tested it face-to-face. The trial took place in November 2026. This was a peer prototype trial, not a study of Year 3 pupils’ learning outcomes.

Respondents

3 TESL trainee teachers — peer testers who tried Detective Duck and checked its usability.

Testing format

2 online testers + 1 face-to-face tester.

Trial date and duration

November 2026.

Testing setup

Mixed-mode peer trial: two online and one in person.

Feedback Gathering Method

Peer feedback and evidence gaps

Prototype testers

Three TESL trainee teachers tried Detective Duck in November 2026: two online and one face-to-face.

Feedback received

Testers identified intermittent recording problems, reading passages that pupils could not consult while answering questions, and limited feedback or reinforcement.

Still to document

The feedback collection format, affected screens, browsers, screenshots, and results of any subsequent retest are not confirmed.

This was peer usability feedback. No Year 3 pupil learning outcomes or formal pre/post-test results are claimed.

CASE FILE 05 / 05

Reflection and Improvement

Three issues reported during the November 2026 peer trial. All three fixes are now reported as completed by the developer; independent retesting is not yet documented.

Improvements During Development
🪪Smoother access

Pupil/teacher sign-in, saved progress and safe exit.

🎧More speaking support

Voice replay, character animation and optional recordings.

📓More pupil choice

Avatar Studio, writing, diary and mini-games.

Peer Trial Feedback · November 2026
Developer-confirmed improvements: All three peer-reported issues have been addressed: recording functions were repaired, reading passages can be accessed during questions, and feedback and reinforcement were improved. Independent retesting has not yet been documented.
🎙️Recording did not always work

Fixed — developer-confirmed. Some recording functions failed during the peer trial; the developer reports that the problems have since been repaired.

📖Reading passages inaccessible during questions

Fixed — developer-confirmed. The developer reports that pupils can now see or revisit the relevant reading passage while answering questions.

💬Limited feedback and reinforcement

Fixed — developer-confirmed. The developer reports that feedback and reinforcement have been improved after the peer trial.

Improvements After Trial

Development refinements and trial-driven changes

Detective Duck has been refined during development through improved role-based login, a student avatar studio, a reflection diary, teacher progress tracking, optional audio recording, character speaking animations, additional mini-games and clearer menu navigation.

Following the November 2026 peer trial, the creator repaired the recording function, added reading-passage access during questions, and strengthened feedback and reinforcement.
Issue identified by peer testersStatus and follow-up
Recording: Some recording functions did not work.Fixed (developer-confirmed): The previously reported recording problems have been repaired.
Passage access: Pupils could not refer to the relevant reading passage while answering questions.Fixed (developer-confirmed): Pupils can now access the relevant reading passage while answering questions.
Feedback: Not much feedback or reinforcement.Fixed (developer-confirmed): The developer reports improved feedback and reinforcement for pupils.
Feedback Analysis

What did the peer testers notice?

Three TESL trainee teachers trialled the prototype in November 2026. Three usability and learning-support issues were reported; no numerical ratings, direct quotations, or pupil performance results have been supplied.

Recording functions

Some recording features did not work during the peer trial.

Access to reading passages

Testers clarified that pupils need the relevant reading passage to remain visible or easy to reopen while answering questions. This is a reading-comprehension support issue, not a request for bibliographic citations.

Reinforcement

Testers felt that the game did not provide enough feedback or reinforcement after learner actions.

Priorities for the next cycle

The three points raised during peer testing were addressed in the revised game.

A small field guide for educators

Teaching with Detective Duck

A flexible lesson route, classroom differentiation, formative assessment suggestions and learner-safe operating notes.

Before entering Quackford

Lesson intention

Audience: Year 3 primary ESL learners (the design targets CEFR A1 Mid).

Core focus: recognising useful words, reading aloud with punctuation, understanding narrative events and retelling the case.

Possible lesson goal: By the end of the learning experience, pupils identify important story vocabulary, read selected sentences with appropriate pauses and sequence five events with support.

Case kit

Before class

Use headphones where possible, check Chrome or another supported browser, consider a pair-work alternative if microphones are restricted and prepare a paper answer sheet for pupils who cannot access the game independently.

Explain that diary entries and avatar names are saved on the device; pupils should use nicknames rather than personal information.

Suggested sequence

One lesson · five learning moments

1
Hook · The missing Golden Quill (5 minutes)

Show the museum scene; ask pupils to predict what happened using simple English.

2
Vocabulary · Find the clues (10 minutes)

Pupils tap highlighted words, listen to models, and practise short meanings in pairs.

3
Fluency · Read with the signs (10 minutes)

Read the case file using yellow commas and red full-stop cues. Model first, then use partner reading.

4
Comprehension · Rebuild the timeline (10 minutes)

Pupils order event cards and compare their thinking before selecting the suspect.

5
Output & reflection (15 minutes)

Pupils write their detective explanation, receive formative feedback and complete “Today I learnt…” in the diary.

Differentiation

Three ways to support every reader

Support

Read together

Use word pictures, teacher read-aloud, sentence frames and a peer. Allow oral responses where suitable.

Core

Investigate with a partner

Read, select evidence and sequence the case using the game prompts. Write a simple supported explanation.

Extension

Be the chief detective

Challenge evidence reliability, write extra descriptive sentences and create a comic or alternative ending.

Formative assessment

Evidence you can gather

EvidenceWhat to look forHow to record
Case DictionaryPupil understands or explains target vocabulary in simple context.Teacher observation / 8-word quick check.
Punctuation Stop SignsPupil pauses appropriately at commas and full stops.Reading checklist / oral observation.
Read-AloudPupil reads sentences with increasing confidence and reasonable phrasing.Short pre/post recording with consent or teacher rubric.
Timeline and interviewsPupil orders events and uses relevant evidence.5-event sequencing record / discussion notes.
Detective writing + DiaryPupil gives a reason, applies sentence conventions and reflects.Work sample / diary response on the pupil device.
